text: “Aferim, old man Velichkov! Look, that’s how I like you. Why should we deceive the young generation? Let’s lay our cards on the table. Ideals! Nonsense! Our own personal earthly satisfaction—that is the ideal we should pursue. I’m glad you’ve already arrived at this truth. And does this vile people deserve us to wear ourselves out for them? While we were younger, that was one thing; but now—we’re men of over forty, we should think about ourselves. Enough of dry bread! Especially you, poor soul, you’ve really suffered in those Istanbul alleys, in those Italian... wasn’t that a whole feat? When you saw Stambolov go berserk, you picked up and left Bulgaria, abandoned those slaves—let them spit in slavery. They’re used to it. You’re not used to suffering, and like any gentleman you did your best to run away. What didn’t your head go through in that cursed Halki—and sometimes even for medicine you didn’t have enough money. Bobchev and Madzharov fell silent. Enough of feats already. And do you know what—go ahead and give up that cursed poetry of yours too. It’s all right, but only when the wind is blowing through your purse; and now, thank God, we’ve more or less settled ourselves. They’ll start now—various brats, various little socialists, little idealists—to bark at you, but don’t let your eye even blink! Pretend not to hear them, look after your pleasure, and while you’re at it, enjoy yourself and sneer at their brains. It’s obvious. Why would they bark at you? Surely because of some betrayal of yours, some fraud, out of disappointment? No! Out of envy? Of course! Without a doubt! Without a doubt, out of envy! And why? Simply because their bones were crushed, their throats were torn, while you (you’re a terrible devil, may the devil take you!) just happened to land ready-made in the warmest place. Well, do you see now? Have you come around? Didn’t I tell you that in this world the best thing is to be warm? This struggle for society, ideals, and I don’t know what nonsense—all of it is rubbish! Just now, when you put your little bag down at the end of the month and they heap fifteen hundred leva on you... A fine thing, damn it! Hold on now! Once you’ve got the bone—hold it! Don’t even think about whose skin those leva were flayed from... Beat the flour sack, damn it! Beat it! It’s letting out...”

But you may wonder why I am writing this letter to you. I am writing it to praise you for your speech the other day in the National Assembly. Well done, Kocho! Honestly, I was moved to tears with joy. I almost came to you and kissed you in front of all the deputies. But then they would start stamping their feet at me, objecting...

Do you remember which speech I mean? How could you not remember? The whole world is talking about it. But you are right, Kocho! What’s the big deal if so many thousands of voters don’t go and tear apart twenty gendarmes and fifty drunken thugs? No big deal! The gendarmes would have shot at most a hundred voters! So what, is that such a big deal? All in all, only about two hundred houses would have been blackened. Let’s say that next Sunday the army comes and shoots, kills at most, at most three hundred people. How many orphaned houses would there be — five hundred houses! Happy holidays!...

Well, those softies have started trying to calm the crowd, so that not a hair on anyone’s head should fall! How can one not be outraged?... Thanks to such spineless softies, you had to wait a full eight years in Halki... To write them so many poems about the stars and about sighs, and for them to make you wait eight years. Eight years! A disgrace to the Bulgarian people. If only at least a hundred thousand voters from all over Bulgaria had gone under the bullets, you could have taken your present warm place much sooner. But what a lousy people! Cowards! What the hell is this legality and freedom for, if not even a thousand voters are to be exterminated?... Hold on, dear Kocho, I like you that way. Give such speeches more often, so as to inspire greater confidence in the big bosses... and then just enjoy yourself! So what if the young generation is going to grumble, so what if the people are going to be stirred up—don’t even blink! The people! The people are a herd; just swing the club at them... And after all, am I the one to teach you these things!...

I am most glad that it was you who hurried to deliver this speech; no one could get ahead of you. And now, if you have not inspired them with trust, where else could you!... All the notables are praising you! “Bravo,” they say, “Kocho has become one of us; at last, sense has come into his head.” So keep your wits about you now, hold on this time, and don’t be afraid!... But still, mind you, Kocho, put some money aside, for one never knows—life is a flower!

Kocho, when you read this letter, tear it up so it doesn’t fall into the hands of that fellow who once described me traveling around Europe, because he’ll print me somewhere again. I heard him the other day speaking to someone: “Well, what a pity, I really didn’t expect those words from our Velichkov...” — and I listened to him and wondered at his mind. The wind blows him about... Kocho, why are you still publishing that damned “Progress”? Give it up! And besides, even its name is so childish; it no longer suits a solid man like you. And if you’re itching to write so much, then write away, but it would be most fitting to call the newspaper “It’s Not the Time,” and for our partisans to call themselves, then, not-the-time-ists.
I brought a few small perfume bottles in my saddlebags. Can’t you whip up some little law so that public buildings can be sprinkled with rose oil?
